The long, hot Dixie summer rules it out entirely, so there is only the one fall sowing here, no summer planting. Keep the seeds and pods away from the kitchen; unlike edible peas, they are poisonous.
sweet-pea.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet pea is not one of USU Extension's Table 1 vegetable rows, so this narrow fall window is carried from the vine's own biology: sow from late September up to the average November 1 first frost, into deep, well-drained soil on a trellis, and cut stems from about mid-November through the mild winter into spring. St. George's summers routinely reach 100°F in June, July, and August, per USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation data, and sweet pea cannot tolerate sustained heat at all, so this is a single fall-sown cycle with no summer planting and no fall replant, unlike the region's more heat-tolerant cool-season crops. Keep it well clear of edible peas in the kitchen: the seeds and pods are poisonous.

bee-balm.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

transplant.label: primary
transplant.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bee balm is set out as a transplant or spring division about a week after the last frost and grown as a hardy returning perennial; St. George's dry summer heat, not winter cold, is the limiting factor for this moisture-loving plant (USU Extension planting-date framework).

bee-balm.plantings_provenance: No USU Table 1 row exists for bee balm (a vegetable-focused chart, not flowers/herbs); this cell follows bee balm's own perennial-in-place archetype (its existing nevada/low_desert_az/warm_arid herbaceous-perennial cell shape: one spring establishment planting, a short bloom window, summer heat exclusion, winter crown dormancy) re-anchored to the St. George frost dates, with the heat_pause sourced to USU's Washington County frost/elevation page's 100°F June-August figure.

8.notes: Bee balm is a hardy returning perennial, but its love of moisture against St. George's extreme dry heat makes it a real stretch: set out a transplant or spring division about a week after the last frost, irrigate heavily and consistently, and give afternoon shade. Expect a short spring bloom before daytime highs push past 100°F and close the season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: June, July, and August are excluded by summer heat: St. George reaches over 100°F in these months (USU Extension, Washington County frost and elevation data), and bee balm is a moisture-loving temperate perennial that stalls in extreme dry heat even with heavy irrigation, so it blooms in the mild spring window before the heat wall and is not carried through the hottest stretch.

bee-balm.region_notes_beginner: Bee balm is a hardy perennial that returns every year in St. George's Dixie, but its love of moisture makes the desert a real stretch: set out a transplant or spring division about a week after the last frost, water generously, and give afternoon shade. Expect a shorter spring bloom before summer's brutal heat shuts it down.
bee-balm.region_notes_seasoned: In St. George's Mojave-edge high desert, bee balm is planted once, about a week after the March 30 average last frost, and returns from its crown each year, but extreme dry heat, not winter cold, is the real limiting factor for this moisture-loving temperate perennial. It blooms in the mild spring window before daytime highs climb over 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension, Washington County frost and elevation data), then rests through the hottest stretch and goes dormant with the return of frost around November 1. Give it heavy, consistent irrigation and afternoon shade.

echinacea.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

transplant.label: primary
transplant.synthesis_note_seasoned: Echinacea is established once from a spring division, transplant, or stratified seedling and grown as a long-lived, drought-tolerant herbaceous perennial that returns from its crown each year; unlike bee balm and mint, it does not need a summer heat_pause in St. George's Dixie once established in full sun and sharp drainage (USU Extension planting-date framework).

echinacea.plantings_provenance: No USU Table 1 row exists for echinacea (a vegetable-focused chart); this cell follows echinacea's own perennial-in-place archetype (its existing nevada/low_desert_az/warm_arid herbaceous-perennial cell shape) re-anchored to the St. George frost dates. Unlike bee balm and mint, echinacea is drought-tolerant and thrives through the St. George summer once established, so no heat_pause is carried (matching the Nevada donor's own divergence for this crop); appropriate siting and deep infrequent watering answer the desert's dryness, not its heat.

8.notes: Echinacea is drought-tolerant and does well in St. George's Dixie once established: set out a division, transplant, or stratified seedling in spring in full sun and sharp drainage, water deeply but infrequently, and it blooms from early summer into fall without the heat exclusion moisture-hungry perennials need here. Leave cones standing into winter for the birds, then cut back in late winter; divide an established clump every 3 to 4 years.

echinacea.region_notes_beginner: Echinacea (purple coneflower) does well in St. George's Dixie: plant one division or transplant in spring in full sun and fast-draining soil, and it comes back every year, blooming from early summer into fall. Unlike bee balm and mint, it is drought-tolerant and does not need a summer break here; water deeply but infrequently and leave the seed heads standing for the birds.
echinacea.region_notes_seasoned: In St. George's Mojave-edge high desert, echinacea is established once, in spring about a week after the March 30 average last frost, from a division, transplant, or stratified seedling, and returns from its crown for years. It is genuinely drought-tolerant and, once sited in full sun with sharp drainage, carries a long bloom from early summer into fall without the summer heat pause the desert's moisture-hungry perennials need. Water deeply but infrequently, avoid soggy soil, and divide an established clump every 3 to 4 years.

mint.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

transplant.label: primary
transplant.synthesis_note_seasoned: Mint is set out as a division, rooted cutting, or transplant (not seed), grown as a contained perennial. In St. George's dry desert climate it runs as a cool-season crop, established in early fall for a harvest that carries through the mild winter and into spring, pausing through the scorching summer (USU Extension planting-date framework; Washington County frost and elevation data).

mint.plantings_provenance: No USU Table 1 row exists for mint (a vegetable-focused chart); this cell follows mint's own perennial-in-place archetype (its existing nevada/low_desert_az/warm_arid herbaceous-perennial cell shape: fall establishment, a long cool-season harvest, summer heat exclusion) re-anchored to the St. George frost dates, with the heat_pause sourced to USU's Washington County frost/elevation page's 100°F June-August figure.

8.notes: Plant one clump inside a pot or a buried, bottomless barrier so mint's spreading roots stay contained. In St. George's dry heat, mint runs as a cool-season crop: establish a division or cutting in early fall, harvest fall through spring, and pause through the extreme summer, when even heavy shade and constant water struggle to keep it going. Keep the soil evenly moist and pinch flower buds to keep leaves tender.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: June, July, and August are excluded by summer heat: St. George reaches over 100°F in these months (USU Extension, Washington County frost and elevation data), and mint is moisture-loving with little drought tolerance, so the dry heat scorches its foliage even with afternoon shade; it is grown as a cool-season, fall-established crop and paused through the hottest weeks.

mint.region_notes_beginner: Mint grows in St. George's Dixie as a cool-season perennial: plant a contained clump (a pot or buried barrier keeps it from spreading) in early fall, harvest through the mild winter and into spring, then let it rest through the scorching summer, when even heavy shade and water struggle to keep the leaves from burning.
mint.region_notes_seasoned: In St. George's Mojave-edge high desert, mint is set out as a division or rooted cutting (not seed) in early fall and grown as a contained returning perennial; unlike temperate climates, it runs on a cool-season calendar here, harvested from late October into spring. Mint's high moisture demand against the region's dry heat is the real desert challenge: even with afternoon shade and constant water, the foliage scorches once daytime highs climb over 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension, Washington County frost and elevation data), so the crop is not carried through that stretch. Keep the soil evenly moist and pinch flower buds for tender leaves.

chamomile.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Chamomile direct-sows into St. George's cool shoulders: a spring window from early March into April, ahead of the region's own hardy-crop planting dates (USU Extension), and again in August for a fall round (Heflebower, Fall Gardening in the St. George Area).

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First bloom about 68 days after sowing, this crop's own days-to-maturity, continuing through each cool window until the summer heat wall.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bloom ends as St. George summer heat arrives or, for the fall cycle, as sustained winter cold sets in.

chamomile.plantings_provenance: Structural donor: chamomile's own nevada/low_desert_az/warm_arid analog cells (a cool-season annual flower/herb pattern, not on any USU vegetable-only planting chart). Shape re-anchored to the St. George frost dates and cited to USU's general vegetable planting-date framework for the spring window and Heflebower's Fall Gardening in the St. George Area for the fall window, since this crop is not a chart-tabled row; the midsummer gap between the two windows is the sourced heat_pause (USU Washington County frost/elevation 100°F figure), and the remaining winter gap renders cold_pause under the region's real frost dates.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: June and July are excluded by summer heat: German chamomile flowers best in mild weather and declines once temperatures push into the upper 90s and 100°F (USU Extension, Washington County frost and elevation data records St. George reaching over 100°F in June, July, and August), so it is grown in the cool shoulders and skipped through the two hottest, driest weeks of midsummer before a fresh sowing resumes in August.

chamomile.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, sow German chamomile in the cool shoulders: early March through April for spring bloom, and again in August for a fall round. Summer's extreme heat and real winter cold both close the door, so this is a two-window desert crop, and it often self-sows.
chamomile.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's Mojave-edge high desert grows German chamomile on two cool-season cycles: a spring sowing (early March through April, ahead of USU Extension's own hardy-crop planting dates) blooms into June, then a real midsummer heat gap once temperatures push over 100°F in June and July (USU Extension, Washington County frost and elevation data), then a fresh August sowing (Heflebower, Fall Gardening in the St. George Area) blooms into late October before winter cold ends the season around the November 1 average first frost.
